clinicalPearls: Congenital syphilis follows transplacental (and occasionally perinatal) transmission of Treponema pallidum from an infected mother, and the risk is highest with untreated early maternal syphilis
It is almost entirely preventable through antenatal syphilis screening and timely maternal treatment with benzathine penicillin, so every case reflects a missed prevention opportunity
Outcomes range from miscarriage, stillbirth, and hydrops to a live-born infant who may be asymptomatic at birth yet still infected

Early congenital syphilis (within the first two years) features include snuffles (infectious nasal discharge), a maculopapular or desquamating rash often involving palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, and periostitis or osteochondritis causing painful pseudoparalysis
Late stigmata (after two years) include Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, a saddle-nose deformity, frontal bossing, and sabre shins

Diagnosis integrates maternal treponemal and non-treponemal serology, comparison of infant and maternal non-treponemal titres, direct detection from lesions or body fluids, and assessment for neurosyphilis
Treatment of the infant is with penicillin, and management must be coordinated with maternal treatment history and adequacy
A confirmed or suspected case mandates public health notification, maternal partner tracing, and evaluation of the mother's own syphilis stage
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital syphilis results when the spirochaete Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta from an infected pregnant woman to the fetus, an event that can occur at any gestation but is most efficient during maternal spirochaetaemia in early (primary and secondary) syphilis. Disseminated fetal infection provokes widespread inflammation and endarteritis affecting the liver, bones, skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system, and the resulting tissue injury underlies presentations from fetal hydrops and stillbirth to the multisystem features of early congenital disease. If the child survives untreated, chronic inflammation and scarring of developing structures such as the teeth, eyes, ears, nose, and long bones produce the classic late stigmata. Maternal treatment before or early in pregnancy prevents fetal infection, which is why antenatal screening is central to control.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital (TORCH) infections such as cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, and herpes simplex
Neonatal sepsis or other bacterial infection
Neonatal hepatitis or haemolytic disease causing jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly
Non-accidental injury or metabolic bone disease as a cause of bony changes and irritability
Blistering or desquamating dermatoses of the newborn
Immune or non-immune hydrops fetalis from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Maternal treponemal and non-treponemal serological testing with review of treatment history
Quantitative non-treponemal titre in the infant compared with the maternal titre
Dark-field microscopy or molecular detection of Treponema pallidum from nasal discharge, mucocutaneous lesions, or placenta
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for cell count, protein, and treponemal testing to assess neurosyphilis
Long-bone radiographs to detect periostitis, osteochondritis, and metaphyseal changes
Full blood count, liver function tests, and additional imaging or ophthalmological and audiological assessment as indicated
Placental and, where relevant, autopsy histopathology in stillbirth
redFlags: Hydrops fetalis, stillbirth, or a severely unwell neonate
Signs of neurosyphilis or abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings
Pseudoparalysis of a limb indicating painful bony involvement
Interstitial keratitis or new sensorineural deafness suggesting active or late disease
Maternal syphilis untreated or inadequately treated before delivery
reference.prognosis: When the mother is screened and adequately treated in good time, fetal infection is usually prevented and the outlook is excellent; established infection treated promptly in the neonate generally does well, but untreated disease carries substantial mortality and, in survivors, irreversible late stigmata such as deafness and dental and skeletal deformity.
pitfalls: Assuming an asymptomatic newborn of an infected mother is uninfected without appropriate evaluation
Judging maternal treatment adequate without confirming the agent, timing, and titre response (only benzathine penicillin given in good time is reliable)
Misinterpreting infant serology, since transplacental maternal antibody can produce a positive result without infection
Overlooking neurosyphilis by not examining the cerebrospinal fluid when indicated
Failing to notify public health services and trace and treat the mother's partners
references: BASHH UK national guidelines on the management of syphilis
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
